vignette:
The Weight of Glass

Marcus is twenty-six years old, and he still flinches at the sound of balloons popping.

Three years ago, Marcus was working the afternoon shift at a mid-sized bank in the city when two armed men entered through the front doors. What followed lasted eleven minutes by the clock, though Marcus has never been able to make those eleven minutes feel like anything less than a lifetime. One of the men fired a shot into the ceiling. Another held a weapon directly at Marcus's face across the teller window. A third accomplice, who had been waiting outside, detonated a small improvised device near the entrance when police arrived — an act later characterized by investigators as a domestic terrorist incident. The explosion shattered the glass partition in front of Marcus, and a fragment opened a cut along his left cheekbone that required fourteen stitches. Two customers were hospitalized. Everyone survived, but Marcus sometimes struggles to feel like that word — survived — fully applies to him.

In the weeks after the incident, Marcus's family, originally from the Philippines and now scattered between two cities, rallied around him. His mother flew in and stayed for a month. His then-wife, Diane, took time off work. People told him he was lucky, and he smiled and agreed, because he did not yet have the language for what was happening inside him. He was not sleeping. When he did sleep, he would wake convinced he could smell smoke. He began checking the locks on the apartment door four and five times before bed, and then again at two in the morning when he got up to stand in the kitchen and wait for his heart rate to slow.

He returned to work at the bank after six weeks because he did not know what else to do. Standing behind the counter again felt like standing inside a photograph of something terrible. Every time a customer approached his window wearing a backpack or a heavy coat, his vision would narrow and his hands would go cold. He developed a habit of tracking the front entrance with his eyes every few seconds — a rhythm so automatic now that he barely notices he is doing it. His supervisor has mentioned it twice, gently, not unkindly. Marcus thanked her and changed nothing, because he cannot.

The marriage ended quietly about a year after the attack. Diane said she felt like she was living with someone who had already left. Marcus did not argue. He had felt himself leaving for some time — pulling back from conversations, from touch, from anything that required him to be fully present in a moment that might suddenly become dangerous. He moved into a studio apartment and found a certain relief in the smallness of it, the single exit he could monitor from the couch.

Now Marcus moves through his days with the particular exhaustion of someone who is always, at some level, braced for impact. He is good at his job — careful, accurate, courteous — and his colleagues would describe him as quiet and professional. What they do not see is the calculation he runs every morning before walking through the bank's front doors: where the exits are, where he would go, what he would do. He has not eaten at a restaurant with his back to the room in three years. He declined an invitation to a friend's Diwali celebration last autumn because he knew there would be fireworks, and he could not explain why that mattered without explaining everything else.

He describes his emotional life as "flat, mostly," interrupted by moments of terror that arrive without warning — a car backfiring, a raised voice in the lobby, the particular quality of afternoon light that sometimes reminds him of that day. He does not talk about the attack often. When he does, he speaks about it in a careful, factual way, as though describing something that happened to someone he used to know.

In a sense, he is.
